pos.personaBrief: Sarriball dominates possession (Chelsea and Napoli regularly dominated the ball, 75% territorial superiority vs Inter) and uses it to defend; Juventus 2019/20 was more pragmatic.

pro.personaBrief: Every attack starts from the back with a secure goalkeeper and a regista (Jorginho), but the passing is vertical and line-breaking, with quick transitions after regains.

est.personaBrief: Rehearsed 4-3-3 automatisms with defined roles per phase, but close combinations, third-man runs, rotations and inside forwards make it relational in attack.

lar.personaBrief: The attacking trio is narrow and attacks infield (Hazard, Mertens) while overlapping full-backs give the width; the build-up is central through the regista and midfield triangles.

blo.personaBrief: High line, aggressive press and immediate counter-press are focal points of Sarriball, with the front players pressing the centre-backs.

mar.personaBrief: Zonal, space-oriented defending with a high line, half-and-half positions and zonal set-piece defending; no man-marking evidence.

pla.personaBrief: Persistent with his model and the same XI, imposing the 4-3-3 on arrival at Napoli, though he adapted to players at Juventus; he says he does not know what Sarriball is.

res.personaBrief: Associated with beautiful, dominant football, with no trophy at Napoli despite 91 points; plays to win away and doesn't park the bus.

sis.personaBrief: System-first: the collective model, refusal to rotate and building around Jorginho show that automatisms make players better, with functions for all.

jog.personaBrief: Technical, intelligent players who read the game (Jorginho, Hamsik, Allan's tenacity as the exception) over physical duels.

bas.personaBrief: Relied on a stable core of established players and resisted turnover; little evidence of youth focus beyond some Chelsea minutes.

lid.personaBrief: Honest and direct, wants players to have fun and bring out their inner child, but ran a demanding system and had friction with players at Juventus and Lazio.
